title: Topic, supporting and concluding sentences
blurb: Build and judge a paragraph: pick the topic sentence, the best support and the right conclusion, and remove the sentence that breaks unity.
question: A paragraph about bilingual nurses includes the sentence “Language classes at community colleges have become more expensive.” Should it stay or go, and how do you decide in seconds on test day?

teach.h: A paragraph is one idea, fully developed
teach.body: Formally, a well-organized paragraph has a topic sentence that states its main idea, supporting sentences that develop that idea, and often a concluding sentence that wraps it up. It must have unity (every sentence relates to the topic), coherence (ideas in a logical order) and development (enough relevant support). Plain English: say what the paragraph is about, prove it, wrap it up, and leave out anything that wanders.

(1) Reading food labels helps shoppers make healthier choices. (2) The label lists the serving size, so buyers can compare products fairly. (3) It also shows sodium and added sugar, two nutrients many people try to limit. (4) The grocery store on Elm Street recently added self-checkout lanes. (5) In just a few seconds, a label can turn a guess into an informed decision.

rows.label: (2) The label lists the serving size ...
(3) It also shows sodium and added sugar ...
(5) A label can turn a guess into ...

teach.note: Sentence 4 mentions a grocery store, but it says nothing about labels or healthier choices, so it breaks unity.

root.label: Supporting sentences
root.sub: Each must back the topic sentence

teach.caption: A true, interesting sentence is still wrong if it does not support THIS topic sentence.

head: Pattern
Order
Signal words
rows: next to, above, at the back

teach.body: A good topic sentence is broad enough to cover every supporting sentence but narrow enough to be one idea: “Community gardens benefit their neighborhoods,” not “Nature matters in life” (too broad) or “Gardeners can trade seeds” (a detail). It usually comes first but can come last. A concluding sentence restates or wraps up the main idea in new words. It never introduces a new topic or contradicts the paragraph.

teach.h: Scenario: Hannah trims her essay paragraph
teach.body: Nursing applicant Hannah Brooks writes: (1) Working as a hospital transporter showed me how much patients rely on nurses. (2) Nurses explained each test before patients left the unit. (3) They noticed small changes, such as a new cough, and acted quickly. (4) The hospital also has a large parking garage for visitors. (5) Watching them, I decided to give that kind of care myself. Sentence 4 shares the word hospital but says nothing about nurses, so she removes it.

teach.text: The sentence to remove is rarely silly. It usually shares a keyword with the topic (language, store, clinic) but makes a different point. Test every sentence against the topic sentence, not against the general subject. And never pick a detail as the topic sentence just because it is the most vivid.

items: Topic sentence: the main idea, broad enough to cover all support, narrow enough to be one idea.
Supporting sentences: examples, facts, explanations, quotations or anecdotes that back the topic.
Concluding sentence: wraps up or restates; no new idea, no contradiction.
Unity: remove any sentence that does not support the topic sentence, even if it shares a keyword.
Coherence: logical order, with claims before examples and nouns before the pronouns that refer to them.
Know the patterns: chronological, spatial, importance, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution.

summary: You can now identify and write topic, supporting and concluding sentences, and judge a paragraph for unity, coherence and development. You can also remove the sentence that breaks unity and name a paragraph's organizational pattern.

A.q: Read the paragraph: “___ Members can quiz one another before exams. They can share notes when someone misses a lecture. Explaining a concept to others also helps students remember it.” Which sentence would make the best topic sentence?
options: Members can also compare answers on homework sets.
Study groups give students several practical advantages.
Many colleges have libraries with group study rooms.
Studying is an important part of every college student's life.
A.why: It states the one idea that every supporting sentence develops: the advantages of study groups.

whyNot.0: It is another supporting detail (note the word also), not the main idea.
whyNot.2: It is about libraries, which the supporting sentences never discuss.
whyNot.3: Too broad: it does not mention study groups at all.

A.q: (1) Our clinic now offers evening hours for working families. (2) Appointments are available Monday through Thursday until 8 p.m. (3) The clinic's parking lot was repaved last spring. (4) Families no longer need to miss work or school to see a provider. Which sentence should be removed to improve unity?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
A.why: The paragraph is about evening hours for working families; the repaved parking lot has nothing to do with that idea.

whyNot.1: Sentence 2 supports the topic with specific days and times.
whyNot.3: Sentence 4 explains the benefit of the new hours and wraps up the idea.

A.q: “Taking short walks during long study sessions can improve focus. A ten-minute walk gives the eyes and mind a break from screens. Returning to the desk after moving around often helps students feel more alert.” Which sentence is the best conclusion?
options: Swimming is another form of exercise that many students enjoy.
Some students, however, prefer to study for hours without a break.
Walking shoes come in many styles and price ranges.
For these reasons, short walks belong in every study plan.
A.why: It wraps up the paragraph's main idea (short walks help studying) without adding a new topic.

whyNot.0: It introduces a new topic, swimming.
whyNot.1: It introduces a contrasting idea at the end instead of concluding.
whyNot.2: It is off-topic: shoes have nothing to do with focus during study.

B.q: Which sentence would best support the topic sentence “Hospital volunteers ease the workload of nursing staff”?
options: Volunteers deliver meals and escort patients to tests.
Many volunteers are retired teachers or college students.
Volunteering looks impressive on a nursing application.
Hospitals are often busiest during the winter months.
B.why: It gives examples of tasks volunteers take off nurses' hands, which directly supports the claim about workload.

whyNot.1: It describes who volunteers are, not how they reduce nurses' workload.
whyNot.2: It is about the volunteer's benefit, not the nursing staff's workload.
whyNot.3: It is about hospital demand, not what volunteers do.

B.q: Which statement about a concluding sentence is correct?
options: It should introduce a new argument to keep readers interested.
It wraps up the main point without adding a new idea.
It must repeat the topic sentence word for word.
It should present the paragraph's strongest statistic.
B.why: A concluding sentence restates or wraps up the main idea and adds no new topic.

whyNot.0: New ideas in a conclusion break unity.
whyNot.2: It restates the idea in new words, not word for word.
whyNot.3: Statistics are support; they belong in the body of the paragraph.

B.q: (A) She then sent the completed form to the admissions office. (B) First, Lena downloaded the application form. (C) Next, she filled in each section carefully. (D) A week later, she received a confirmation email. Which order makes the paragraph most logical?
options: B, A, C, D
C, B, A, D
B, C, A, D
B, C, D, A
B.why: Chronological order: download (B), fill in (C), send (A), get confirmation (D). The words first, next, then and a week later confirm it.

whyNot.0: She cannot send the completed form before filling it in.
whyNot.1: Next cannot come before First, and she must download the form before filling it in.
whyNot.3: The confirmation cannot arrive before she sends the form.

C.q: (1) Bilingual nurses improve care in diverse communities. (2) They can explain medication instructions in a patient's first language. (3) Language classes at community colleges have become more expensive. (4) They can also help patients describe symptoms accurately. (5) As a result, patients often feel more comfortable and better understood. Which sentence should be removed?
options: Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 5
C.why: Sentence 3 shares the word language but is about class costs, not about how bilingual nurses improve care.

whyNot.0: Sentence 2 gives a direct example of improved care.
whyNot.2: Sentence 4 gives a second example of improved care.
whyNot.3: Sentence 5 states the result and concludes the paragraph.

C.q: “The most important reason to get a flu shot is to protect people with weak immune systems. Another reason is to avoid missing work or classes. A final, smaller benefit is shorter lines at the clinic later in the season.” Which organizational pattern does this paragraph use?
options: Chronological
Spatial
Compare and contrast
Order of importance
C.why: The reasons move from most important to least important, signaled by “most important,” “another” and “a final, smaller.”

whyNot.0: The reasons are ranked, not told in time order.
whyNot.2: Nothing is being compared or contrasted; all three are reasons for one action.

C.q: (1) Maria reviews her flash cards on the bus. (2) She answers practice questions during her lunch break. (3) Before bed, she rereads one lesson summary. (4) Maria has found ways to fit studying into a busy schedule. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
C.why: Sentence 4 states the general idea that sentences 1 to 3 illustrate. Here the topic sentence comes last (specific to general).

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 is one specific example of how she studies.
whyNot.2: Sentence 3 is a third specific example.

reteach.title: A paragraph is a table
reteach.question: Picture a tabletop held up by legs. What does the tabletop stand for, what are the legs, and what happens if one leg is under a different table?

blocks.h: Tabletop, legs and a finished edge
blocks.body: The topic sentence is the tabletop: the main idea everything else holds up. Each supporting sentence is a leg, and it only helps if it is under THIS table. A leg standing under the next table (an off-topic sentence) holds up nothing, so you remove it. The concluding sentence is the finished edge: it tidies what is there and does not bolt on a new table.

blocks.h: Which legs hold up the table?

root.label: Topic: Food labels help shoppers choose

blocks.text: A leg can look right because it is made of the same wood (it shares a keyword). Check whether it actually supports the tabletop.

explain.body: The topic sentence states the paragraph's one main idea. It is general enough to cover every supporting sentence but not so broad that it could cover anything.

test.q: Which sentence would work best as a topic sentence rather than a supporting detail?
options: Night shifts bring unique challenges for new nurses.
At 3 a.m., the hospital cafeteria is usually closed.
Most night shifts at the hospital last twelve hours.
Many nurses drink coffee to stay alert overnight.
test.why: It states a general idea that the other three sentences could support.

whyNot.1: A specific detail that could support the topic of night-shift challenges.
whyNot.2: A specific fact, not a main idea.
whyNot.3: A specific detail about coping, not the main idea.

explain.body: Support must back the exact claim in the topic sentence. Ask: does this sentence help prove the topic sentence?

test.q: Topic sentence: “Packing a lunch saves students money.” Which sentence best develops it?
options: A homemade sandwich costs less than most cafeteria meals.
Packing a lunch takes about ten minutes each morning.
Some students prefer a hot meal in the middle of the day.
The campus cafeteria opens at 11 a.m. on weekdays.
test.why: It directly supports the claim about saving money by comparing costs.

whyNot.1: It is about time, not money.
whyNot.2: It is about preference, not savings.
whyNot.3: It is about cafeteria hours, not cost.

explain.body: A concluding sentence restates or wraps up the main idea in fresh words. It does not add a new topic or reverse the argument.

test.q: Which is the best concluding sentence for a paragraph arguing that clinics should offer weekend hours?
options: Some clinics also offer telehealth visits in the evening.
However, weekday hours are more popular with clinic staff.
Weekend hours would make care easier for working families.
Clinics are buildings where patients go to see providers.
test.why: It restates the argument for weekend hours and wraps it up with the main benefit.

whyNot.1: Introduces a counterpoint that undercuts the argument at the end.
whyNot.3: A general definition that does not wrap up the argument.

explain.body: Unity means every sentence supports the topic. Coherence means the order is logical: claims before examples, time order for events, and a noun before any pronoun that refers to it.

test.q: (A) For example, a brisk walk can ease tension after a long exam. (B) Regular exercise is one of the simplest ways to manage stress. (C) Even five minutes of stretching can help. Which sentence should come first?
options: Sentence A
Sentence B
Sentence C
Any of them
test.why: Sentence B states the claim; A and C are examples that must follow the claim they illustrate.

whyNot.0: “For example” needs a claim before it.
whyNot.2: “Even five minutes” assumes the reader already knows the claim about exercise.
whyNot.3: The order matters: an example cannot come before its claim.
